survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2009 and PISA 2018 data and conducts country-level analyses where each country is weighted by its 15-year-old population size (i.e., larger countries contribute more than smaller ones). The paper explicitly contrasts this approach with the standard practice of assigning equal weights to all countries in cross-national PISA studies. No student-level complex survey weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) is reported in the provided text; therefore, the extraction cannot confirm whether PISA sampling weights were applied at the student level. The analytic unit is the country, and the outcomes are per-country change scores (2009 to 2018), so the key weighting described is population-size weighting at the country aggregation stage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this paper are per-country change scores in reading literacy and in awareness of reading strategies, plus correlations/regressions among these aggregated change measures. The text does not describe any plausible-value (PV) workflow (e.g., Rubin’s rules) or missing-data handling strategy for the underlying PISA cognitive scores. Because the analysis is conducted at the country level using aggregated change indicators rather than an explicit PV-based student-level modeling pipeline, PV handling is not applicable from the information provided, and missing-data handling is not reported in the excerpt.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2009 and PISA 2018 for 15-year-olds, with countries as the unit of analysis. Included only countries that participated in both years and for which reading literacy data were available in 2018; Spain was excluded because 2018 reading literacy data were not available. The outcomes are per-country differences between 2009 and 2018: change in online chatting frequency, change in reading literacy, and change in awareness of reading strategies. Country-level data were weighted by population size (15-year-old population) when computing descriptive statistics and regression/correlation results.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation (r) between change in online chatting and change in reading literacy: −0.718 (p = .000). Regression (analysis 1): beta = −0.718, R² = 0.515; unstandardized coefficient: −0.642 reading points per 1 percentage-point increase in chatting frequency; p = .000. Regression (analysis 3, joint model): beta for online chatting = −0.491, R² = 0.674; unstandardized coefficient: −0.439 (p = .000).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 and 2018 data for 15-year-olds’ reading literacy at the country level, the study leveraged online chatting change to predict per-country change in reading literacy, finding that increases in online chatting were strongly associated with declines in national reading averages (r = −0.718; regression beta = −0.718, R² = 0.515). This indicates that rapid growth in online chatting coincides with meaningful deterioration in reading literacy at the system level, suggesting that reading-strategy support may need to be strengthened alongside digital communication trends, though the study is correlational and cannot establish causality.

main_findings.target_variable: Mediation: indirect effect of online chatting change via reading-strategy awareness change
main_findings.performance_metrics: Structural equation modeling: total effect of change in chatting on reading literacy = −0.718 (analysis 1), decomposed into direct effect = −0.491 and indirect effect = −0.494 × 0.458 = −0.226; total effect equals direct + indirect.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 and 2018 data for 15-year-olds’ reading literacy at the country level, the study leveraged online chatting change and reading-strategy awareness change to model direct and indirect pathways, finding that part of the negative association between chatting and reading literacy is mediated through declines in awareness of reading strategies (indirect effect = −0.226; direct effect = −0.491). This indicates that strengthening students’ metacognitive/strategy awareness may be a key lever for mitigating reading declines associated with expanding online chatting, though the mediation is based on correlational country-level change rather than causal identification.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2009 & 2018 (15-year-olds) Awareness of reading strategies (country-level change)
main_findings.target_variable: Per-country change in awareness of reading strategies (2009→2018)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation between change in online chatting and change in awareness of reading strategies: r = −0.494 (p = .000). Regression (analysis 4): beta = −0.494, R² = 0.244; unstandardized coefficient: −0.003 (p = .000).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009 and 2018 data for 15-year-olds’ awareness of reading strategies at the country level, the study leveraged online chatting change to predict per-country change in awareness of reading strategies, finding a strong negative association (r = −0.494; regression beta = −0.494, R² = 0.244). This indicates that countries with larger increases in online chatting also show declines in students’ awareness of useful reading strategies, implying that educational practice should explicitly teach and reinforce strategy awareness to counteract potential distraction effects of digital communication, while causality remains uncertain.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2009 and PISA 2018 reading literacy and questionnaire measures for 15-year-olds, aggregating to the country level and analyzing per-country change over 2009–2018. It reports that the rise in online chatting frequency is strongly negatively correlated with change in reading literacy (r = −0.718, p = .000) and with change in awareness of reading strategies (r = −0.494, p = .000). Regression results show that online chatting change predicts reading literacy change with beta = −0.718 and R² = 0.515 in the bivariate model, and beta = −0.491 with R² = 0.674 when jointly modeled with strategy awareness change. Structural equation modeling further indicates mediation: the total effect (−0.718) is split into a direct effect (−0.491) and an indirect effect (−0.226). The analysis is correlational (no individual-level change), and the excerpt does not document PV handling or missing-data procedures for the underlying PISA cognitive scores.
